video_title: The Stock Market Is Doing the Fed’s Job
gist: Ben Evans of Fed Watch Advisors argues Nvidia's selloff alone equated to ~1.5 Fed hikes of tightening, so the stock market is doing the Fed's job: he sees a 25bp December hike as locked in but a January skip likely. He flags AI credit stress in neoclouds like CoreWeave (GPU prices vs token prices as the trigger), doubts consumer AI monetization, and prefers IBM, AMD, Google and Microsoft over edge plays like SanDisk and CoreWeave.

themes.theme: Stock market as Fed tightening proxy

insights.claim: Ben Evans calculated, using the Fed's financial-conditions framework (a percentage change in equities equated to 25bp of hikes/cuts), that Nvidia's stock decline alone over the past week equated to roughly one and a half Fed rate hikes of tightening.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Nvidia's index weight makes its drawdowns a macro tightening event; watch NVDA volatility as a real-time gauge of financial conditions.
insights.quote: I calculated that the Nvidia move alone just the stock alone moving down accounted almost for one and a half rate hikes by the Fed

insights.claim: Because Nvidia sits in every ETF and carries large index weight, its volatility is now systemic: sharp NVDA drawdowns signal the stock market is pricing in Fed tightening on the Fed's behalf.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Treat NVDA drawdowns as de facto policy tightening that may reduce the need for further Fed hikes.
insights.quote: the stock market is doing it for the fed

insights.claim: The US economy has shifted from a credit/consumption economy to an AI-driven investment economy, which brings higher growth and productivity, therefore structurally higher rates, more speculation, and more volatility.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Position for a higher-rate, higher-volatility regime rather than a return to low-rate consumption-led growth.
insights.quote: We're now I think really in an investment economy as opposed to years ago more of a credit consumption economy

insights.claim: A 20-30% equity decline puts the AI investment cycle itself in doubt and hits consumer spending via the wealth effect, so the stock market is effectively driving the economy right now.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Equity drawdowns feed back into capex and consumption data with a lag; expect macro data to soften after market shocks.

insights.claim: The economy is so financialized that policymakers (the administration and possibly the Fed) will not let an AI-led selloff 'run into an abyss'; the president's intervention to bring Jensen Huang back was a signal the administration does not want the capex cycle derailed.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Implies a policy put under the AI complex; sharp selloffs may be met with intervention.
insights.quote: we can't let it run into an abyss because the economy is too financialized

themes.theme: Fed path: hike locked, then pause

insights.claim: Fed officials (over 22 speakers in a week, with Waller notable) have been hawkish, messaging that inflation is too far above target and risks de-anchoring toward 3%, while deliberately letting markets do part of the tightening rather than slamming the brakes with something like a 100bp hike.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Fed communication is itself a tightening tool; hawkish Fed-speak plus market drawdowns substitute for larger hikes.
insights.quote: let signal to the markets this is our clear intent and let the markets do part of our job

insights.claim: Ben Evans views a 25bp Fed hike at the December 9 FOMC meeting as locked in given sticky inflation, and floated 50bp for debate, noting the minutes showed some members leaning that way if inflation does not improve.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Rate-sensitive positioning should assume a December hike; upside risk of 50bp if PCE/inflation data disappoint.
insights.quote: So this rate hike is locked in

insights.claim: Ben Evans's updated call is that market-driven tightening has been so large (multiple hikes' worth) that the Fed can hike in December and then skip January, moving one step at a time as it did when it skipped October.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Look for a pause in January; front-end rates may overprice a staircase of consecutive hikes.

insights.claim: If the Fed does not hike in December, stocks would get short-term relief but long yields would pop, and markets would re-price tightening if inflation does not improve; Ben Evans has a 6% 10-year yield call, which the host called aggressive.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: A dovish surprise is a bear-steepener risk; any equity relief rally may be short-lived.
insights.quote: We go higher with the 10ear yield. You know, my call right at 6%.

insights.claim: A Q4 2018-style Fed pivot is unlikely because then inflation was below target and the escalating China trade war raised deflation risk; today inflation is above target and the bigger wild card is the war in Iran, not a China trade war.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Don't bet on a Fed put via pivot after the 20% selloff analog; the macro setup differs.
insights.quote: We're in a totally different situation today. We're above target.

insights.claim: Upcoming ISM, PMI and construction data will likely still be strong but will begin to reflect the October-November market shock, while the unresolved Iran conflict (crude around $80, ships being attacked) remains a risk factor.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Watch December macro prints for first signs of shock transmission into activity.

insights.claim: Credit risk in AI sits not with the hyperscalers themselves but with less well-capitalized companies financed through them, a stress that started with Oracle, moved to CoreWeave, and then to names like AMD and Micron.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Monitor credit spreads and single-name CDS of AI-levered borrowers as the stress transmission channel.

insights.claim: CoreWeave has a roughly $23 billion market cap against about $66 billion of debt, with some unsecured debt trading at junk levels, and neoclouds would be first to lose contracts if AI demand disappoints.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: Neocloud equity and debt are the highest-beta, most fragile expression of AI demand risk.
insights.quote: It's got a $23 billion market cap. It's got $66 billion in debt.

insights.claim: Ben Evans calculates the internal rate of return on a GPU at over 22% because compute demand is enormous and there is no GPU glut yet; a GPU glut or falling GPU values would put CoreWeave in big trouble given its debt-heavy balance sheet backed mainly by Nvidia.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Track GPU rental prices (and the forthcoming CME GPU derivatives) as the key leading indicator for neocloud solvency.
insights.quote: the internal rate of return on the GPU is over 22%

insights.claim: The key stress signal is the divergence between falling token prices and rising GPU rental prices; if GPU prices start falling sharply due to oversupply, the AI ecosystem comes under stress. CME is planning GPU derivatives that would let investors trade this.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Watch token price vs GPU rental price spread; a GPU price break is the trigger for AI credit stress.

insights.claim: AI financing differs from pre-GFC SPVs: it appears to be largely conventional bond issuance rather than opaque AAA-labeled structured products, and credit markets show essentially no stress yet, though off-balance-sheet debt is opaque and should be watched.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Don't assume a GFC replay; but watch single-name CDS, credit-spread options and financing channels for building stress.
insights.quote: there seems to be zero stress really building there yet

insights.claim: Markets punish hyperscalers (e.g. Meta, Google) when they announce higher capex funded by borrowing, which Ben Evans interprets as the stock market pricing in credit risk.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Capex-guidance-up announcements are near-term negative catalysts for hyperscaler stocks.

insights.claim: Ben Evans's 'Genron' framing: the SEC is examining accounting tied to Nvidia's Singapore operation, the first critical look at how Nvidia derives GPU profits in competitive markets, though he does not believe Nvidia is inflating profits.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Regulatory scrutiny of Nvidia's Asia channel sales is a tail risk to monitor for revenue quality.

themes.theme: GPU oversupply and AI premium deflation

insights.claim: Jensen Huang's reported comment about an 'avalanche of wafers and memory' and Nvidia's push to sell into Asian markets via Singapore/Malaysia suggests supply may outrun US frontier-lab demand, raising risk of a GPU oversupply as Asian competition drives prices down.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: Semis are cyclical; overbuilding of GPUs and data centers is likely and would compress margins.
insights.quote: we have an avalanche of wafers and memory coming in

insights.claim: Overbuilding in semis and data centers is inevitable in this cycle, and the AI valuation premium will deflate as growth rates normalize and competition rises; the recent selloff was the first sign of that reassessment.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Expect multiple compression for AI leaders even if the capex cycle continues.

insights.claim: Nvidia's growth rates will by definition decline (host cites ~100% this year, ~70% expected next), though Jensen's strategy of selling into Asia within export-control boundaries keeps producing upside surprises.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Decelerating growth vs. continued beats is the core tension in NVDA's multiple.

insights.claim: AI subscriptions work like a newspaper model; the broad consumer will not pay for extra tokens for everyday tasks like trip planning and will revert to free Google search, limiting consumer AI monetization to niche power users.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Consumer AI revenue assumptions may be too high; profit expectations tied to compute-shortage pricing will come under pressure.

insights.claim: Microsoft Office 365 (about 450 million users, ~20 million Copilot subscribers cited) and Google's free, search-subsidized suite are the templates OpenAI and Anthropic will likely converge on: broad use at low, discounted fees.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Expect frontier-lab pricing to fall toward mass-market levels, pressuring per-user revenue.

insights.claim: Anthropic has traded poorly post-IPO because investors question how it will build a global subscription market and become the AI benchmark the way Microsoft became the software benchmark; investors are in 'show me' mode ahead of its first earnings call.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Anthropic's first earnings call is a key catalyst for pure-play AI sentiment; OpenAI IPO may follow within months.

insights.claim: Meta stock rallied about 30% after introducing Muse as an implied monetization engine despite a capex raise from $135B to $140B, then gave it all back as investors questioned the actual monetization model.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: AI monetization narratives without disclosed economics are not sticky for stock prices.

insights.claim: Ben Evans sees AI ecosystem selloffs as buying opportunities as long as the capex cycle is not derailed by regulation or Fed hikes, with commitments in the trillions of which only an estimated few hundred billion (up to ~$400 billion) has entered the economy this year.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Pick spots in the AI complex on drawdowns, mindful of credit risk.
insights.quote: selloffs like this are opportunities you know pick your spots

insights.claim: AMD and Micron look cheap because earnings growth forecasts remain robust; Micron is said to trade around 3.5x forward earnings, though the host notes Micron had negative gross margins about three years ago and is highly cyclical.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Low multiples on cyclical memory names may be peak-earnings traps; the bull case relies on capex not slowing.
insights.quote: micron I believe is trading at three and a half times forward earnings

insights.claim: Ben Evans would avoid the extreme AI-risk names like SanDisk and CoreWeave, which need more compensation for risk than current prices offer, and prefers IBM (cheap, transforming into an AI company) and AMD (market has shown willingness to rotate leadership from Nvidia to AMD).
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Barbell away from levered AI edge plays toward cheaper, diversified AI beneficiaries.
insights.quote: Sandex is maybe the extreme aversion. I don't want to be really playing there.

insights.claim: Rather than pure-play Anthropic, Ben Evans prefers diversified AI exposure via IBM, Google, and Microsoft, plus Apple as an AI-light hedge and industrials, utilities and financials (e.g. GE Vernova, GE) as part of the AI capex cycle.
insights.speaker: Ben Evans (Fed Watch Advisors)
insights.so_what: Construct AI portfolios with second-derivative industrial/utility exposure and an AI-light anchor like Apple.
